title: The Elements of Mazatec Witchcraft
author: Jean Bassett Johnson
summary: A Berkeley anthropologist's field survey of Mazatec witchcraft from a 1938 expedition to Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca. It describes mushrooms eaten by brujos for divination, alongside ololiuhqui and Salvia divinorum, noting mushrooms were never sold openly in markets.
excerpt: "While the brujo is under the influence of the narcotic mushroom, it is the mushroom which speaks, and not the brujo."
citation: Johnson, Jean Bassett. "The Elements of Mazatec Witchcraft." Ethnologiska Studier 9 (Göteborg: Göteborgs Etnografiska Museum, 1939): 128–150.
rights: In copyright (published 1939). Full text digitized and hosted by the Internet Archive; used here only as a short verified excerpt per this project's pre-1930 hosting rule.

_No transcript hosted (text postdates 1930 and is not a US Government work). Excerpt below verified against the Internet Archive scan of Etnologiska Studier 9, pp. 128–150._

"Mushrooms are also eaten by the brujos of Mazatlan, as is general throughout the entire Mazatec area... While the brujo is under the influence of the narcotic mushroom, it is the mushroom which speaks, and not the brujo... Throughout the whole of the Mazatec area, the articles of witchcraft, save the mushrooms, are sold openly in the markets."

draft.rationale: Written directly out of the 1938 Huautla expedition that produced the first outsider-witnessed velada; it is the earliest professional ethnographic account to set the sacred mushroom alongside ololiuqui and Salvia divinorum as a single regional complex of divinatory plants, and to note the mushroom's uniquely restricted, non-commercial status.
